title: Partial isometries and polar uniqueness
subtitle: G2 lecture 038000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: The part of a map that really moves
slides.lead: A partial isometry preserves lengths only on its initial space.
body: For a linear map U, the initial space is M = (ker U)⊥. On M, U preserves inner products and lengths. On ker U it vanishes. The image N = ran U is its final space.
The definition is tailored to polar decomposition: a map may discard some input directions, yet carry every surviving direction to its output without additional stretching.
slides.takeaway: Initial space: surviving inputs. Final space: their length-preserving images.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · The part of a map that really moves

slides.title: The two support projections
slides.lead: The adjoint makes both sides of a partial isometry visible.
body: For x in M, U*U x = x because U is isometric there. For x in ker U, the composition vanishes. Thus U*U is exactly the orthogonal projector onto M.
Similarly UU* acts as identity on ran U and zero on its perpendicular complement. The two projections need not have the same ambient domain when U maps between different spaces.
slides.takeaway: U*U identifies the input support; UU* identifies the output range.

slides.title: A rank-one example
slides.lead: Let U(x,y) = (y,0) on the real plane.
body: U kills the horizontal axis and sends the vertical unit vector to the horizontal unit vector without changing length. Its initial space is the vertical axis; its final space is the horizontal axis.
In matrices, U*U = diag(0,1) and UU* = diag(1,0). Both are orthogonal projections, even though U itself is neither self-adjoint nor a projection.
slides.takeaway: The input and output supports can be different subspaces.

slides.title: What the equation A = U|A| determines
slides.lead: The modulus |A| already tells us which directions survive.
body: Because ran |A| = (ker A)⊥ in finite dimensions, the factorization A = U|A| forces the value of U on that support: U(|A|x) must equal Ax.
Nothing in the product U|A| tests U on vectors orthogonal to ran |A|. The canonical choice therefore imposes the extra condition that U vanish on ker A.
slides.takeaway: The zero-on-kernel rule makes the polar factor canonical.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · What the equation A = U|A| determines

slides.title: Why the canonical polar factor is unique
slides.lead: Uniqueness holds among partial isometries whose kernel equals ker A.
body: Suppose U and W have this property and both satisfy A = U|A| = W|A|. On ran |A| the equality forces U = W, since every element of that range has the form |A|x.
On ker A, both vanish by hypothesis. In finite dimensions the source is the orthogonal direct sum of ran |A| and ker A. Hence U and W agree everywhere.
slides.takeaway: Factorization plus the canonical kernel condition fixes the polar factor.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · Why the canonical polar factor is unique

slides.title: Unitary completion is generally nonunique
slides.lead: For A = diag(2,0), its modulus is A and its canonical polar factor is diag(1,0).
body: The identity matrix also satisfies A = I|A|, but it acts differently on the kernel. In the real plane, diag(1,−1) is another orthogonal factor with the same product.
The factorization determines the motion along the first axis only. Asking for a full orthogonal or unitary extension introduces an independent choice on the unused complement.
slides.takeaway: A unitary factorization need not have a unique unitary factor.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · Unitary completion is generally nonunique

slides.title: When does a completion exist?
slides.lead: The unused input and output directions must have compatible dimensions.
body: The canonical factor maps (ker A)⊥ isometrically onto ran A. To make a full unitary, one must also map ker A isometrically onto (ran A)⊥.

For a square finite-dimensional matrix the two unused spaces have equal dimensions by rank–nullity. A unitary extension therefore exists, but the isometry chosen between these complements is not unique.
slides.takeaway: Completing the partial motion is a matching problem on the defect spaces.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · When does a completion exist?

slides.title: Changing signs keeps lengths
slides.lead: Negating A reverses every output while preserving every output length.
body: The modulus cannot detect that sign: (−A)*(−A)=A*A. The canonical polar factor can detect it, because on the initial space the output directions must reverse.
Consequently, replacing A by −A preserves its modulus but negates its canonical polar factor. This comparison separates magnitude data from motion data in a concrete way.
slides.takeaway: The modulus carries stretch; the polar factor carries orientation and placement.

slides.title: Real signs and complex phases
slides.lead: The freedom in completing a rank-deficient polar factor depends on the scalar field.
body: For A=diag(2,0) in the real plane, an orthogonal completion must fix the first axis and may send the second axis to itself or its negative. These are two different orthogonal factors with the same product A=V|A|.

Over the complex numbers, any unit-modulus phase may be placed on the unused one-dimensional kernel. The unitary completion is therefore a continuous family, but the canonical partial isometry remains diag(1,0).
slides.takeaway: Kernel freedom is discrete for real one-dimensional defects and continuous for complex ones.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 038000 · Real signs and complex phases

slides.title: Reconstruct the proof
slides.lead: To recover polar uniqueness, establish what is determined on the support and what is free off it.
body: Compute U*U and UU* for U(x,y)=(y,0). Then compute the modulus and canonical polar factor for A=diag(2,0). Verify directly that distinct orthogonal extensions give the same product A=V|A|.
Finally, explain why an extension is possible precisely when the remaining source and target dimensions match. No reference to a particular eigenbasis is needed.
slides.takeaway: Canonical partial isometries and chosen full unitaries solve different uniqueness questions.
